background.definition: Frozen shoulder, a term that is synonymous with adhesive capsulitis, is a condition of uncertain etiology characterized by significant restriction of both active and passive shoulder motion that occurs in the absence of another known intrinsic shoulder disorder.

list.listitem: Prevalence in the general population is slightly greater than 2%.
Approximately 70% of those affected are women.

Primary adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder) is idiopathic. The etiology has yet to be fully understood, but it is said to include contracture or shortening of the capsule and glenohumeral ligaments.
Secondary adhesive capsulitis has a known cause such as recent history of rotator cuff surgery. Typical antecedents include trauma, overuse, or postsurgical stiffness.
Pathophysiology is not clearly understood.
Disagreement exists as to whether the underlying cause is an inflammatory process or a fibrosing process, although some studies now suggest that it is both, depending on the stage of the disease.
Differentiate between restriction in active versus passive ROM (patients with adhesive capsulitis have both). It is important to stabilize the scapula when checking for ROM. C
Radiographs should be ordered to rule out other common causes, especially in patients with recent trauma. C
Consider adhesive capsulitis in diabetic patients who present with unilateral idiopathic shoulder pain. C
Patients typically present after trauma or immobilization, complaining of decreased ROM of the shoulder.
Symptoms and examination findings may differ based on presenting stage of the disease (see ).
Consider adhesive capsulitis in diabetic patients who present with unilateral idiopathic shoulder pain.
Isolate the glenohumeral joint when testing abduction. Place your hand on the acromion to prevent scapular movement during motion.

Pain may limit a true assessment of passive ROM. Anesthetize the shoulder with an intraarticular injection of 1% lidocaine without epinephrine. Limitations in passive ROM will persist in the case of adhesive capsulitis.
Shoulder radiographs are recommended to rule out other causes of shoulder pain and immobility. Include anteroposterior views in internal and external rotation, axillary views, and outlet views.

Arthrography is considered the gold standard but is rarely done. The normal shoulder will accept 15 to 18 mL of contrast medium. The diagnosis of adhesive capsulitis is made when the joint accepts less than 10 mL.
MRI may be performed when rotator cuff pathology cannot be ruled out by physical examination, but the MRI is not needed for diagnosis of adhesive capsulitis.

Diagnosis is made with history and physical examination. Passive ROM is limited, typically 90° or less of passive abduction is present. Internal rotation is to the sacrum, typically 50% of external rotation is lost.

Order radiographs to rule out other causes of reduced ROM. Absence of recent trauma, decreased passive ROM, and no other clear cause on radiographs makes adhesive capsulitis the most likely diagnosis.
If injection of glenohumeral joint with anesthetic improves ROM significantly, adhesive capsulitis is unlikely, so other causes should be considered.
NSAIDs may have some benefit early in the disease to reduce pain, especially before exercise or physical therapy. C
Physical therapy (PT) is the first-line therapy for adhesive capsulitis. B
Intraarticular corticosteroid injections (CSI) may reduce pain and increase ROM early in the disease process, although the time to full recovery is unchanged. B
Image-guided CSI has similar outcomes compared to injection without image guidance. B
CSI combined with PT may be superior for early symptom reduction than either one alone. B
A large RCT found no clinically significant benefits of manipulation under anesthesia and/or arthroscopy compared to physical therapy at 12 months.B
Consider surgery if more than 90° of abduction is lost or if no response to conservative treatment is evident after 6 months. C
NSAIDs are recommended to relieve pain but have not been shown to alter the disease process. They are especially helpful before therapy or exercises.
Opioid analgesics may be needed in the early stages to relieve pain.

Intraarticular corticosteroid injections (CSI) proved to be superior to physical therapy for reduction of pain in one study when given early in the disease process, although no change in the long-term function was seen. Use of an anterior glenohumeral approach is thought to provide better accuracy.

Ultrasound-guided injections may seem more accurate than anatomical landmark-guided injections, but pain and functional outcomes are similar. Most studies are small and of low quality. A Cochrane review concluded that image-guided CSI has similar outcomes compared to injection without image guidance. Comparable outcomes include pain relief (moderate-certainty evidence), function & quality of life (low-certainty evidence), and adverse events (low-certainty evidence). Given the added costs, the authors of the review recommended against routinely using image guidance for intraarticular CSI to treat adhesive capsulitis.

A systematic review and network meta-analysis of pharmacological interventions for early-stage adhesive capsulitis found intraarticular CSI and intraarticular platelet-rich plasma (PRP) to be the most effective interventions to reduce pain and improve function in the short-term (3 months). However, given the risk of bias, heterogeneity, and inconsistency in the included studies, these results need to be interpreted with caution and more rigorous trials are needed before CSI and PRP are routinely recommended for early-stage frozen shoulder treatment.

In an RCT of 40 patients that compared three sets of CSI with oral prednisolone, the injection group reported better function, ROM, and satisfaction at one year of follow-up compared with the oral steroid group, though both groups improved and there were no differences in reported pain level at any point.

A small study showed some improvement in pain symptoms with oral steroids, but no change in full recovery of ROM. A Cochrane review found low to moderate quality evidence that oral steroids may improve pain, function, and ROM for patients with adhesive capsulitis for up to 6 weeks. Repeated use of systemic steroids may increase adverse events, hence it is not routinely recommended.
No large prospective studies have shown that surgery decreases time to full recovery.
Surgery may be indicated for patients who present during stage 2 or stage 3. A number of surgical approaches may be considered.

Arthroscopic capsular release: This is becoming the surgery of choice because it allows for the visualization of the glenohumeral joint and precise release of the capsule. Some surgeons will perform arthroscopy in combination with manipulation. Small, uncontrolled studies have shown promising results.

Closed manipulation under anesthesia: Due to the risks of humeral fracture, dislocation, and rotator cuff rupture, arthroscopic capsular release is preferred. Contraindications include severe osteopenia, a history of fracture or dislocation, and neurologic injury.

Open surgical capsular release: This option is considered when patients fail to improve following either arthroscopic capsular release or closed manipulation. Disadvantages include postsurgical stiffness, lengthened postoperative recovery time, decreased pain control, and restrictions on physical therapy and rehabilitation exercises.

A pragmatic 3-arm RCT comparing manipulation under anesthesia, arthroscopic capsular release, and early structured physical therapy found no clinically significant differences between groups after 12 months.

Acupuncture: One small study showed a slight short-term benefit in shoulder function with acupuncture when compared with sham acupuncture. Another small study showed that acupuncture plus exercise was better than exercise alone for improving pain, ROM, and function for up to 5 months. A third small study suggested that bee venom acupuncture plus physiotherapy reduced pain and disability at 12 weeks compared with physiotherapy alone.

Physical therapy has been shown to decrease symptoms and should be the first step in the treatment of all patients. However, a Cochrane review found insufficient evidence for or against physiotherapy interventions for adhesive capsulitis, citing variable methodological quality, study heterogeneity, variability in interventions that were used, and length of followup. While some interventions may be beneficial for specific cases, physiotherapy in general has uncertain benefits.

Additionally, a Cochrane review found that CSI may be more effective than manual therapy and exercise in the short-term. After arthrogaphic distension with corticosteroids & saline (see below), adding manual therapy and exercise may improve patient-reported treatment success and active ROM. What is not known is whether adding manual therapy and exercise as adjunctive therapy after CSI results to improved outcomes.
A small, single-center randomized trial found no difference in outcomes between a smartphone-assisted rehabilitation and a traditional self-exercise program.
A Cochrane review found low to moderate quality evidence that arthrographic distension using saline, air, and/or steroids may improve pain, function, and ROM in the short-term.

Failure of nonsurgical options
Adhesive capsulitis is a self-limiting disease with a natural history of 18 to 36 months. C
Most patients regain 90% of their original ROM by 18 months regardless of treatment. C
Patients who have not shown a progressive improvement should be referred to orthopedic surgery. C
Recurrence of adhesive capsulitis in the same shoulder is rare. C
Patients are at increased risk of developing adhesive capsulitis in the contralateral shoulder. C

feature.caption: Stages in the Presentation of Adhesive Capsulitis.

tr.td: Months 0-3. Pain, achy at rest and sharp at extreme ROM, night pain and progressive loss of internal rotation, forward flexion, abduction and a subtle loss of external rotation and adduction
Months 3-9. Chronic pain with active and passive ROM; significant limitation of forward flexion, abduction, and internal and external rotation
Months 9-15. Minimal pain except at the end of ROM, but still with significant limitation in ROM
Months 15-24. Minimal pain and progressive improvement in ROM
